items.title: I can define fallibility and explain how it applies to perception
items.what: Fallibility is the quality of being prone to error or experiencing difficulties in judgement. Applied to perception, it means that our brain's processing of sensory information can produce inaccurate experiences even when the sensory organs themselves are working normally.
items.why: Recognising that fallibility is a normal feature of perception prevents students from assuming that perceptual errors always indicate a disorder or defect. It frames the entire topic correctly before specific examples are introduced.
items.example: A person with perfect vision still consistently perceives one line in the Muller-Lyer illusion as longer than the other, even after being told they are equal in length. The eye is functioning normally; the error is in the brain's interpretation.

subtopic.name: Fallibility of Perception
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the concept that both visual and gustatory perception are prone to error in normally functioning individuals. It distinguishes between errors occurring at the level of sensation versus errors occurring during the brain's processing and interpretation of sensory information.
subtopic.why: Understanding that perceptual errors are normal and expected challenges the assumption that our senses give us a perfectly accurate picture of reality. This foundation is essential for making sense of all the specific phenomena studied throughout the chapter.

items.title: I can define perceptual distortion and distinguish it from a sensation error
items.what: A perceptual distortion is an error in the judgement or interpretation of sensory stimuli. It differs from a sensation error in that the sensory organs detect information accurately, but the brain misinterprets or misrepresents that information during the perception stage.
items.why: This distinction is critical for exam responses. Many students confuse agnosia, spatial neglect, and illusions with problems in the eye or ear, when in fact the distortion occurs during perception in the brain.
items.example: A patient with visual agnosia can see a toothbrush clearly (normal sensation) but cannot identify what object it is (distortion during perceptual interpretation). The eye is not at fault.

items.title: I can identify the three general sources of visual illusions
items.what: Visual illusions can arise from environmental sources (features of the physical world that make interpretation difficult), physiological sources (biological processes in the eyes or brain that create misleading signals), or psychological sources (personal biases, expectations, and prior learning that shape interpretation).
items.why: Knowing these three categories allows students to correctly classify and explain unfamiliar illusions in exam questions, not just the specific examples studied in class.
items.example: The moon appearing larger near the horizon is an environmental illusion. An afterimage following a bright flash is physiological. Susceptibility to the Muller-Lyer illusion being greater in people raised in built environments is psychological or social.

items.title: I can explain that perceptual distortions occur in healthy brains and do not indicate a malfunction
items.what: Experiencing perceptual distortions, including illusions, synaesthesia, or spatial neglect caused by a lesion, does not mean that the brain is fundamentally broken or that perception is useless. These phenomena demonstrate the dynamic, interpretive nature of perception rather than a catastrophic failure.
items.why: Students need this perspective to write balanced evaluation responses, and it reflects the nuanced scientific understanding that normality and abnormality exist on a continuum.
items.example: Every person with normal vision will be fooled by the Ames room illusion when viewing it through a peephole with one eye, because the room is deliberately designed to exploit the brain's normal visual processing rules.

items.title: I can define a visual illusion using precise terminology
items.what: A visual illusion is the perception of a visual stimulus that conflicts with how it actually is in physical reality. It is not caused by a problem with the eyes but arises during the brain's processing of visual information.
items.why: The definition must specify that the conflict is between perception and physical reality, and that the sensory organs are functioning normally. Exam questions often test whether students can distinguish illusions from problems of sensation.
items.example: In the Muller-Lyer illusion, both lines are physically identical in length (measurable reality), but one is consistently perceived as longer (perception). This conflict between reality and experience defines it as a visual illusion.

subtopic.name: Visual Illusions
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines visual illusions as a demonstration of the fallibility of visual perception. It covers the definition of visual illusions, the Muller-Lyer illusion and its psychological and environmental explanations, and the Ames room illusion and the visual constancies it manipulates.
subtopic.why: Visual illusions provide clear, testable, everyday evidence that normally functioning brains systematically misinterpret sensory information. Understanding the specific mechanisms behind named illusions prepares students for both recall and application questions in assessment.

items.title: I can describe the Muller-Lyer illusion and what makes it effective
items.what: The Muller-Lyer illusion presents two lines of equal length, one with inward-pointing arrowheads and one with outward-pointing arrowheads. The line with outward-pointing arrowheads is consistently perceived as shorter, and the one with inward-pointing arrowheads as longer, despite being identical.
items.why: The Muller-Lyer illusion is the key named example in the study design and is frequently used in exam questions that ask students to describe, explain, or evaluate a visual illusion.
items.example: When two horizontal lines are drawn with arrowheads at each end, and the arrowheads on the left line point inward while those on the right point outward, most people perceive the right line as longer even after measuring both and confirming they are the same length.

subtopic.name: Visual Illusions
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines visual illusions as a demonstration of the fallibility of visual perception. It covers the definition of visual illusions, the Muller-Lyer illusion and its psychological and environmental explanations, and the Ames room illusion and the visual constancies it manipulates.
subtopic.why: Visual illusions provide clear, testable, everyday evidence that normally functioning brains systematically misinterpret sensory information. Understanding the specific mechanisms behind named illusions prepares students for both recall and application questions in assessment.

items.title: I can explain the psychological (carpentered world) explanation for the Muller-Lyer illusion
items.what: Richard Gregory (1968) proposed the carpentered world hypothesis: when people see the lines, they unconsciously apply depth cues from built environments stored in memory. The inward-arrowhead line resembles the outward corner of a building (closer, extending toward the viewer), while the outward-arrowhead line resembles the inward corner of a room (further away). This misapplication of linear perspective and depth cues causes the size difference to be perceived.
items.why: This explanation demonstrates how prior learning and memory (psychological factors) directly shape perception, linking the illusion to broader concepts of top-down processing and perceptual sets.
items.example: A person who has grown up in a city with angular buildings and rooms automatically processes the arrowhead lines as three-dimensional corners. The line that looks like an outward-facing building corner appears to extend toward them, so the brain judges it as larger.

items.title: I can explain the environmental or social explanation for the Muller-Lyer illusion
items.what: Research by Ahluwalia (1978) showed that people living in urban, built-up environments were more susceptible to the Muller-Lyer illusion than people from rural, uncarpentered environments. This suggests that exposure to angular, built environments strengthens the learned associations that drive the illusion.
items.why: This explanation demonstrates that perceptual experience can be shaped by the environment a person grows up in, providing a cultural and social dimension to what might otherwise seem like a universal biological response.
items.example: In a study with participants from Zambia, those living in cities were more often fooled by the Muller-Lyer illusion than those living in rural areas with fewer rectangular buildings, suggesting the illusion depends partly on cultural visual experience.

items.title: I can describe the Ames room illusion and identify what makes it work
items.what: The Ames room is a specially constructed room that appears rectangular when viewed through a peephole with one eye, but is actually trapezoid in shape. One back corner is much further from the viewer and the ceiling is twice as high on the left. Two people standing in the room appear dramatically different in size even though both are of normal height.
items.why: The Ames room illustrates how strongly visual constancies govern perception, and how deliberately exploiting the physical environment can cause predictable and dramatic perceptual errors.
items.example: A person viewing the Ames room through a peephole sees one adult appearing to be roughly the size of a small child standing next to another normal-sized adult. The illusion disappears if the viewer uses both eyes or is allowed to move their head.

subtopic.name: Visual Illusions
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines visual illusions as a demonstration of the fallibility of visual perception. It covers the definition of visual illusions, the Muller-Lyer illusion and its psychological and environmental explanations, and the Ames room illusion and the visual constancies it manipulates.
subtopic.why: Visual illusions provide clear, testable, everyday evidence that normally functioning brains systematically misinterpret sensory information. Understanding the specific mechanisms behind named illusions prepares students for both recall and application questions in assessment.

items.title: I can explain how the Ames room manipulates size constancy and shape constancy
items.what: Size constancy is the ability to perceive an object as remaining the same size even as it moves further away and projects a smaller image on the retina. Shape constancy is the ability to perceive an object as maintaining the same shape even when viewed from different angles. The Ames room defeats size constancy by hiding the true distance of the person in the far corner, and defeats shape constancy by disguising its trapezoid shape as a rectangle.
items.why: Understanding which specific visual constancies are being exploited provides the mechanistic explanation for why the illusion works, which is required for higher-order exam responses.
items.example: Because the viewer cannot perceive that the person on the left is standing much further away (size constancy is blocked by the deceptive room design), the brain interprets the smaller retinal image as a genuinely smaller person rather than a normal person at a greater distance.

subtopic.name: Visual Illusions

It covers the definition of visual illusions, the Muller-Lyer illusion and its psychological and environmental explanations, and the Ames room illusion and the visual constancies it manipulates.
subtopic.why: Visual illusions provide clear, testable, everyday evidence that normally functioning brains systematically misinterpret sensory information. Understanding the specific mechanisms behind named illusions prepares students for both recall and application questions in assessment.

items.title: I can define agnosia using the correct terminology
items.what: Agnosia is a disorder involving the loss or impairment of the ability to recognise familiar stimuli through the use of one or more senses, despite the senses functioning normally otherwise. In visual agnosia, a person can see clearly but cannot identify what they are looking at.
items.why: The definition must emphasise that the senses themselves remain intact. This is a common point of confusion in exams, where students incorrectly attribute agnosia to a vision problem rather than a perceptual processing problem.
items.example: A person with visual agnosia walks past their car in a car park because they cannot recognise it, even though their visual acuity is tested as normal and they can see the colour, shape, and size of the vehicle clearly.

subtopic.name: Agnosia
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers agnosia as a disorder of visual recognition in which otherwise normally functioning vision fails to allow identification of familiar objects or people. It distinguishes the two main subtypes, apperceptive and associative visual agnosia, and examines the neurological causes and characteristic experiences of the condition.
subtopic.why: Agnosia demonstrates that the ability to recognise objects is a distinct cognitive process that can be selectively damaged, showing that perception involves more than just clear sight. It also illustrates how brain lesions in specific regions produce specific perceptual deficits.

items.title: I can identify and describe the common neurological causes of agnosia
items.what: Agnosia is typically caused by a brain lesion, which is a point of damage to the brain. Lesions may result from stroke, dementia, traumatic brain injury, brain tumour, or overexposure to a toxin. Visual agnosia is commonly associated with lesions in the parietal, temporal, or occipital lobes, which are involved in processing visual information.
items.why: Understanding the neurological basis of agnosia reinforces the idea that it is a disorder of brain processing, not of sensory input, and connects the topic to broader material on brain structure and function.
items.example: Patient JPM developed associative visual agnosia following a heart attack that deprived parts of his brain of oxygen, creating a brain lesion. His neurological functioning, visual field, and MRI scan were all otherwise normal.

subtopic.name: Agnosia
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers agnosia as a disorder of visual recognition in which otherwise normally functioning vision fails to allow identification of familiar objects or people. It distinguishes the two main subtypes, apperceptive and associative visual agnosia, and examines the neurological causes and characteristic experiences of the condition.
subtopic.why: Agnosia demonstrates that the ability to recognise objects is a distinct cognitive process that can be selectively damaged, showing that perception involves more than just clear sight. It also illustrates how brain lesions in specific regions produce specific perceptual deficits.

items.title: I can distinguish between apperceptive and associative visual agnosia
items.what: Apperceptive visual agnosia involves difficulty in perceiving the form or visual elements of an object, meaning the person cannot construct a coherent visual representation of what they are seeing. Associative visual agnosia involves intact perception of visual elements but an inability to link that perception to prior knowledge or memory, so the person cannot assign meaning or identity to what they see.
items.why: These two subtypes are directly referenced in the study design and frequently appear in exam case study questions. Students must be able to identify which type is being described and distinguish the key difference: perception is impaired in apperceptive agnosia but intact in associative agnosia.
items.example: A person with apperceptive agnosia shown a drawing of a dog cannot copy the drawing accurately. A person with associative agnosia shown the same drawing copies it accurately but cannot say what the animal is or whether it is real or invented.

subtopic.name: Agnosia
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers agnosia as a disorder of visual recognition in which otherwise normally functioning vision fails to allow identification of familiar objects or people. It distinguishes the two main subtypes, apperceptive and associative visual agnosia, and examines the neurological causes and characteristic experiences of the condition.
subtopic.why: Agnosia demonstrates that the ability to recognise objects is a distinct cognitive process that can be selectively damaged, showing that perception involves more than just clear sight. It also illustrates how brain lesions in specific regions produce specific perceptual deficits.

items.title: I can apply knowledge of agnosia subtypes to describe the abilities and difficulties of a person with each type
items.what: A person with apperceptive agnosia struggles to perceive the overall form of an object, so they cannot draw it, copy it, or group it with similar objects, even though their sight is technically intact. A person with associative agnosia can perceive and describe individual features (colour, shape, size) and can copy images accurately, but cannot name, categorise, or identify what they are seeing.
items.why: Exam questions frequently present a case study and ask students to predict what abilities and difficulties a patient would display. Being able to apply this distinction accurately is essential for scoring well on application questions.
items.example: Patient C.K., who had associative visual agnosia, could correctly answer 'does the dog have a long or short tail?' and 'what colour is its fur?' when shown an image of a dog, but was completely unable to identify what animal he was looking at.

items.title: I can explain why agnosia is classified as a perceptual disorder rather than a sensory disorder
items.what: In agnosia, the sensory process of vision is intact: light enters the eye, the retina responds, and signals travel to the brain normally. The failure occurs during the perceptual stage when the brain attempts to interpret and assign meaning to the visual information it has received.
items.why: This explanation is required when evaluating whether visual perception should be trusted, or when comparing agnosia with conditions that affect sensation. It also supports the broader argument that perception is an active, brain-based process.
items.example: Dr. P, the patient described by Oliver Sacks, could see clearly and recognised people by voice and movement, yet could not recognise faces visually or identify common objects by sight, demonstrating that his eyes were not the source of his difficulties.

items.title: I can define supertasters and describe their key biological characteristics
items.what: Supertasters are individuals who have a significantly low threshold for taste stimuli and an unusually high number of taste buds (papillae) on the tongue. They are particularly sensitive to bitter tastes and were identified by Linda Bartoshuk (1994), who found that approximately 25% of people showed extreme sensitivity to the bitter chemical PROP.
items.why: Supertasters demonstrate that biological differences between individuals lead to genuinely different taste experiences, even when tasting the same food. This is a named example in the study design.
items.example: A supertaster eating a piece of dark chocolate with 85% cocoa may find it overwhelmingly bitter and unpleasant, while a non-supertaster eating the same piece finds it pleasantly intense. The supertaster's papillae density means more taste receptor contact per bite.

subtopic.name: Fallibility of Gustatory Perception
subtopic.what: This subtopic explores the ways in which taste perception is prone to error or individual variation, including genetic differences in taste sensitivity (supertasters), chemical manipulation of taste receptors (miraculin), and the influence of non-taste factors such as perceptual set, colour intensity, and texture on how flavours are judged.
subtopic.why: Gustatory perception is often assumed to be straightforward and reliable, but this subtopic reveals that taste is deeply shaped by biology, expectations, and other senses. Understanding these influences has practical implications for food science, marketing, and health behaviour.

items.title: I can explain why the experience of supertasters is not classified as a perceptual distortion
items.what: A perceptual distortion is an error in the interpretation of sensory stimuli. Supertasters' heightened sensitivity occurs at the level of sensation (more taste buds means more sensory receptors detecting the chemical signals), not during the brain's interpretation of those signals. Their perception is accurate relative to the sensory input they receive.
items.why: This distinction is a common exam question and requires students to understand the difference between sensation-level differences and perception-level distortions. Supertasters are not experiencing an error; they are accurately perceiving a more intense sensory signal.
items.example: If two people eat the same piece of broccoli and one tastes bitterness twice as intense as the other, that is because the supertaster has more papillae detecting more bitter compounds. They are not misinterpreting the signal; they are receiving a stronger one.

subtopic.name: Fallibility of Gustatory Perception
subtopic.what: This subtopic explores the ways in which taste perception is prone to error or individual variation, including genetic differences in taste sensitivity (supertasters), chemical manipulation of taste receptors (miraculin), and the influence of non-taste factors such as perceptual set, colour intensity, and texture on how flavours are judged.
subtopic.why: Gustatory perception is often assumed to be straightforward and reliable, but this subtopic reveals that taste is deeply shaped by biology, expectations, and other senses. Understanding these influences has practical implications for food science, marketing, and health behaviour.

items.title: I can describe how miraculin alters taste perception and the mechanism by which it works
items.what: Miraculin is a protein extracted from the miracle berry that makes sour foods taste sweet. It binds to the taste receptors on the tongue that are responsible for detecting sweet flavours and activates them when an acidic (sour) environment is created in the mouth. It does not change the functioning of the sour taste buds themselves.
items.why: Miraculin is a named example in the study design and illustrates how the perceptual experience of taste can be deliberately manipulated through a chemical mechanism. It reinforces the idea that taste perception is not a fixed, objective reading of food.
items.example: A person who eats a miracle berry tablet and then bites into a lemon perceives the lemon as tasting sweet rather than sour. The lemon has not changed; miraculin has activated the person's sweet receptors in response to the acid in the lemon juice.

subtopic.why: Gustatory perception is often assumed to be straightforward and reliable, but this subtopic reveals that taste is deeply shaped by biology, expectations, and other senses. Understanding these influences has practical implications for food science, marketing, and health behaviour.

items.title: I can explain how perceptual set influences the judgement of flavours and give an example
items.what: A perceptual set is a predisposition to perceive certain features of sensory stimuli while ignoring others, shaped by expectations, past experiences, beliefs, and culture. When applied to taste, a perceptual set can cause a person to rate the flavour of food differently based on non-taste information such as branding, packaging, or prior reputation, creating a perceptual distortion.
items.why: Perceptual set is a key concept across multiple areas of the unit, and its application to taste demonstrates how psychological and social factors can override objective sensory information. It also connects to the study of top-down processing.
items.example: In a study by Bellizzi and Martin (1982), participants rated the same jelly as tasting better when it was labelled as a name brand than when labelled as a generic brand, even though the jelly was physically identical in both jars.

items.title: I can explain how colour intensity influences flavour judgement
items.what: More intensely coloured food or drink is generally perceived as having a stronger or more intense flavour, even when the actual chemical composition of the flavour is identical to a less intensely coloured version. This is because prior experience has established an expectation that brighter colour indicates greater ripeness or flavour concentration.
items.why: This phenomenon demonstrates how visual information from one sense can override or reshape the experience of another sense (taste), illustrating the interconnected and interpretive nature of perception.
items.example: Studies by Johnson and Clydesdale (1982) and Roth and colleagues (1988) found that a more deeply coloured drink was rated as tasting sweeter than a paler drink of identical sugar content, showing colour intensity acting as a false cue for sweetness.

subtopic.why: Gustatory perception is often assumed to be straightforward and reliable, but this subtopic reveals that taste is deeply shaped by biology, expectations, and other senses. Understanding these influences has practical implications for food science, marketing, and health behaviour.

items.title: I can describe two ways that texture influences the perception of flavour
items.what: First, texture affects the intensity of flavour by determining how much of the food contacts taste receptors and for how long. Liquid foods expose more surface area to receptors than solid forms of the same food. Second, texture affects the enjoyment of flavour through expectations about how a food should feel, which are informed by prior experience.
items.why: Understanding the two-pathway influence of texture (intensity through receptor contact, and enjoyment through expectation) allows students to give precise and complete answers about how texture operates, including identifying which of the two constitutes a perceptual distortion.
items.example: Orange juice generally tastes more intensely orange than eating an orange segment because the liquid form contacts more taste receptors per sip (intensity, not a perceptual distortion). Soft crackers taste worse than expected because they violate the expectation of crunchiness (enjoyment distortion via expectation).

subtopic.what: This subtopic explores the ways in which taste perception is prone to error or individual variation, including genetic differences in taste sensitivity (supertasters), chemical manipulation of taste receptors (miraculin), and the influence of non-taste factors such as perceptual set, colour intensity, and texture on how flavours are judged.
subtopic.why: Gustatory perception is often assumed to be straightforward and reliable, but this subtopic reveals that taste is deeply shaped by biology, expectations, and other senses. Understanding these influences has practical implications for food science, marketing, and health behaviour.

items.title: I can identify which influences on flavour judgement constitute perceptual distortions and which do not
items.what: Perceptual set and colour intensity both constitute perceptual distortions because they cause the brain to misinterpret the actual sensory signal from food. The intensity aspect of texture is not a perceptual distortion because the change in flavour experienced is caused by a real difference in how much of the food contacts taste receptors. The enjoyment aspect of texture may be considered a distortion when expectations override the actual sensory experience.
items.why: Exam questions regularly ask students to evaluate whether a given phenomenon is or is not a perceptual distortion, requiring a precise understanding of where in the sensation-perception chain the change occurs.
items.example: Rating a wine as tasting better because the label says it is expensive is a perceptual distortion (expectation changes interpretation). Finding that blended fruit tastes more intensely fruity than whole fruit is not a distortion (more receptor contact is a real sensory difference).

items.title: I can define synaesthesia using correct terminology
items.what: Synaesthesia is a perceptual phenomenon characterised by the experience of unusual perceptions in one sensory system after another sensory system has been activated. It is not a mental health disorder and can occur in people with healthy, intact brains.
items.why: The definition must specify that it is the perception (not the sensation) of a secondary sense that is triggered, and that the secondary sensory system has not actually been stimulated by any external input.
items.example: A person with sound-colour synaesthesia hears a car horn and simultaneously perceives the colour red in their visual field, even though no red light or object has entered their visual system. Their auditory system triggered a visual perception.

subtopic.name: Synaesthesia
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers synaesthesia as a perceptual phenomenon in which stimulation of one sensory system triggers an involuntary, automatic perception in a second sensory system that has not been directly stimulated. It examines the key characteristics of synaesthesia, the most common forms, and proposed neurological explanations.
subtopic.why: Synaesthesia demonstrates that perception is a highly individualised, brain-generated experience and that sensation and perception are genuinely distinct processes. It provides a compelling example of perceptual distortion in otherwise healthy individuals.

items.title: I can describe four key characteristics of synaesthesia
items.what: Synaesthesia is automatic and cannot be controlled or prevented. It is generally a one-way process (activating sense A triggers sense B, but activating sense B does not trigger sense A). It is consistent over time (the same stimulus triggers the same secondary perception). And it is unique to the individual (two people with the same type of synaesthesia will likely have different specific associations).
items.why: These characteristics are important for distinguishing genuine synaesthesia from imagination, sensory mixing due to drugs, or simple metaphorical description. They also appear directly in exam questions.
items.example: A synaesthete who sees the number 4 as green will always see it as green, cannot choose to see it as red, and will not see the number 4 when looking at the colour green, illustrating the consistent, automatic, and one-directional nature of the experience.

subtopic.name: Synaesthesia
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers synaesthesia as a perceptual phenomenon in which stimulation of one sensory system triggers an involuntary, automatic perception in a second sensory system that has not been directly stimulated. It examines the key characteristics of synaesthesia, the most common forms, and proposed neurological explanations.
subtopic.why: Synaesthesia demonstrates that perception is a highly individualised, brain-generated experience and that sensation and perception are genuinely distinct processes. It provides a compelling example of perceptual distortion in otherwise healthy individuals.

items.title: I can identify and describe the three most common forms of synaesthesia relevant to this topic
items.what: Grapheme-colour synaesthesia involves seeing colours when looking at letters or numbers. Sound-colour synaesthesia involves seeing colours in response to sounds. Lexical-gustatory synaesthesia involves tasting a specific flavour when reading or hearing a specific word.
items.why: These three forms are directly listed in the textbook and are relevant to both visual and gustatory perception, linking synaesthesia to both sensory systems covered in the study design.
items.example: A person with lexical-gustatory synaesthesia may taste garlic every time they read or hear the word 'train'. The taste is involuntary, consistent, and occurs regardless of whether any food is present.

subtopic.name: Synaesthesia
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers synaesthesia as a perceptual phenomenon in which stimulation of one sensory system triggers an involuntary, automatic perception in a second sensory system that has not been directly stimulated. It examines the key characteristics of synaesthesia, the most common forms, and proposed neurological explanations.
subtopic.why: Synaesthesia demonstrates that perception is a highly individualised, brain-generated experience and that sensation and perception are genuinely distinct processes. It provides a compelling example of perceptual distortion in otherwise healthy individuals.

items.title: I can explain the two-step process by which synaesthesia occurs
items.what: First, a sensory stimulus is detected by one sensory system in the normal way. Second, during perception in the cerebral cortex, information from a second sensory area of the brain is integrated as though it belongs to the same experience, even though that second sense has received no actual stimulation.
items.why: This process-level explanation is required for extended response questions and demonstrates an understanding of where in the sensation-perception sequence synaesthesia operates.
items.example: When a person with synaesthesia sees the letter A (detected by the visual system normally), the brain during perception also integrates information from the olfactory cortex, producing the experience of smelling bananas, even though no banana scent is present in the environment.

subtopic.name: Synaesthesia
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers synaesthesia as a perceptual phenomenon in which stimulation of one sensory system triggers an involuntary, automatic perception in a second sensory system that has not been directly stimulated. It examines the key characteristics of synaesthesia, the most common forms, and proposed neurological explanations.
subtopic.why: Synaesthesia demonstrates that perception is a highly individualised, brain-generated experience and that sensation and perception are genuinely distinct processes. It provides a compelling example of perceptual distortion in otherwise healthy individuals.

items.title: I can explain what synaesthesia demonstrates about the relationship between sensation and perception
items.what: Synaesthesia demonstrates that sensation and perception are two genuinely distinct processes. Two people can receive identical sensory input (e.g. both see the letter A) yet have entirely different perceptual experiences (one sees only A, the other sees A and smells bananas). This shows that perception is highly subjective and constructed by the brain, not a simple readout of sensory data.
items.why: This insight is a key conceptual takeaway of the entire chapter and connects to the broader study design outcome requiring students to understand the subjective, constructed nature of perception.
items.example: A non-synaesthete and a synaesthete both look at the same page of text in identical lighting. The same photons enter both their eyes. Yet one person reads black letters on white paper while the other experiences a vivid landscape of colours associated with each letter.

items.title: I can identify at least one proposed neurological explanation for synaesthesia
items.what: One proposed explanation is that synaesthetes undergo less synaptic pruning during development than non-synaesthetes. Synaptic pruning normally eliminates underused neural connections to make brain functioning more efficient. If fewer synapses are pruned, unusual connections between sensory areas of the brain may remain active, allowing one sense to trigger activity in another.
items.why: While the causes of synaesthesia remain uncertain and contested, knowing at least one proposed mechanism is required for extended response questions and demonstrates an understanding that synaesthesia has a structural neurological basis.
items.example: If the neural connections between the visual cortex (processing letters) and the gustatory cortex (processing taste) are not pruned during childhood development, seeing the word 'pear' may continue to activate the gustatory cortex, producing the taste of pear as a perception.

items.title: I can define spatial neglect using precise terminology
items.what: Spatial neglect is an inability to perceive, report, or orient to sensory information located within one side of space. It is an attentional disorder affecting perception rather than a defect of vision itself, meaning the eyes function normally but the brain fails to attend to one half of the visual field.
items.why: The definition must emphasise that the deficit is in perception and attention, not in vision. Students who describe it as blindness or an eye problem will lose marks in assessments.
items.example: A person with spatial neglect of the left visual field will consistently fail to eat food from the left side of their plate, not because they cannot physically see it but because their brain does not attend to or register that side of space during perception.

subtopic.name: Spatial Neglect
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines spatial neglect as a perceptual disorder in which a person fails to perceive, report, or orient to sensory information located on one side of their visual field, despite having otherwise normally functioning vision. It covers causes, the contralateral nature of the deficit, behavioural manifestations, and clinical tests used to diagnose the condition.
subtopic.why: Spatial neglect provides a clear, real-world example of a perceptual distortion that is observable in behaviour and measurable by clinicians. It also reinforces the concept of contralateral brain processing and the distinction between sensory and perceptual failure.

items.title: I can identify the neurological cause of spatial neglect and explain its contralateral nature
items.what: Spatial neglect is caused by a brain lesion, most commonly resulting from a stroke, neurodegenerative disease, or traumatic brain injury. The deficit occurs contralaterally, meaning damage to the right hemisphere of the brain produces neglect of the left visual field, and vice versa. Spatial neglect most frequently results from damage to the right parietal lobe.
items.why: The contralateral nature of spatial neglect is directly linked to the contralateral processing of visual information established elsewhere in the unit. It is commonly tested in case study questions where students must predict which visual field will be neglected based on lesion location.
items.example: Drew suffered a stroke causing a lesion in her right hemisphere. Because visual processing is contralateral, her left visual field is now neglected. She consistently looks to the right during conversation and fails to notice objects placed to her left.

items.title: I can describe three observable behavioural signs of spatial neglect
items.what: People with spatial neglect commonly display a persistent gaze drift toward the side of the brain that has the lesion. They may fail to dress or groom one side of their body (for example, shaving only one side of the face or putting a shoe on only one foot). They may also eat food only from one side of a plate, failing to register the food on the other side.
items.why: Behavioural signs are important for case study analysis questions and for explaining why the condition is often noticed by family or carers before the patient themselves, which is a common exam question.
items.example: Daryl, who has had spatial neglect for 10 years due to a right hemisphere lesion, routinely shaves only the left side of his face, eats only from the right side of his plate, and bumps into objects on his left side, having adapted his life around an ongoing perceptual deficit.

items.title: I can describe three clinical tests used to diagnose spatial neglect and predict typical results
items.what: The line bisection task asks patients to mark the midpoint of a line: a patient with neglect will mark significantly off-centre toward the non-neglected side. The target cancellation task asks patients to cross out a specific shape across a page; patients with neglect cross out shapes on only one side. The copying task asks patients to reproduce a drawing; patients with neglect omit features from one side of the image.
items.why: These tests are named examples in the textbook and commonly appear in extended response questions. Students should be able to describe the test procedure and predict what a neglect patient's result would look like compared to a typical result.
items.example: A patient with left-side spatial neglect asked to copy a drawing of a clock face will draw a circle and then crowd all twelve numbers onto the right side of the clock, leaving the left side blank or drawing only a partial face.

items.title: I can compare spatial neglect and synaesthesia as examples of perceptual distortions in healthy individuals
items.what: Both synaesthesia and spatial neglect are perceptual distortions that occur in people with otherwise normally functioning senses. However, they differ in several ways. Synaesthesia involves multiple sensory systems and adds extra perceptual information; spatial neglect involves primarily vision and removes access to part of the visual field. Synaesthesia can be present from birth; spatial neglect cannot be innate and is always acquired through brain injury.
items.why: Comparison questions between synaesthesia and spatial neglect are directly featured in the textbook questions and are likely to appear in SAC or exam assessments. Students need to identify at least one similarity and one difference accurately.
items.example: Both a synaesthete who tastes flavours when reading words and a spatial neglect patient who ignores their left visual field have normally functioning eyes and tongues. However, the synaesthete gains an additional involuntary experience while the spatial neglect patient loses access to part of their perceptual world.

subtopic.what: This subtopic examines spatial neglect as a perceptual disorder in which a person fails to perceive, report, or orient to sensory information located on one side of their visual field, despite having otherwise normally functioning vision. It covers causes, the contralateral nature of the deficit, behavioural manifestations, and clinical tests used to diagnose the condition.

items.title: I can explain why spatial neglect patients often do not notice their own condition
items.what: Because spatial neglect is a perceptual distortion rather than a sensory impairment, patients do not experience a blank or dark area in their vision. The neglected side simply does not enter their awareness at all, so there is no obvious sensation of absence to alert them that something is wrong. This is why family members and carers typically notice the condition first.
items.why: This point is directly tested in exam questions asking students to explain why loved ones often recognise spatial neglect before the patient does. It also reinforces the core concept that perceptual distortions can affect awareness without any obvious sensory gap.
items.example: A patient with right hemisphere damage and left-side spatial neglect does not experience darkness or blurring on the left. Their world simply appears complete from their perspective; they have no awareness that an entire half of their environment is being ignored by their brain during perception.
